slides.subline: Imun Seolnongtang — boiling ox bones in Jongno since around 1904, and the answer the city's own 2011 investigation arrived at

items.d: Ox leg bones worked for hours until the broth turns opaque and milky. It arrives unseasoned, which is the point of the next slide.
The usual distinction drawn in Korean food writing: more brisket and less bone, so the liquid stays browner and thinner.
Same house, different cut. On this menu at 18,000 won against 15,000 for the standard bowl, per Korean listing platforms in September 2026.

slides.title:
A century
is a hard thing
to document
slides.body:
Plenty of Korean restaurants claim to be the oldest. This is the one a city government went and checked.

The records, as summarised on Wikipedia from Korean press, put the opening around 1904, under the Korean Empire, from a founder known only as a man surnamed Hong. Yu Won-seok bought the place in 1960; her son Jeon Seong-geun has run it since 1981. The regulars included Sohn Kee-chung, who won the 1936 Olympic marathon, and enough athletes that they jokingly named themselves the Imun Society.

What it has not kept is the building. The house stayed in its colonial-era premises until redevelopment pushed it out in 2011, and a grease fire in the kitchen vents closed it again in October 2023. It is open now, in Gyeonji-dong, listed in the MICHELIN Guide as a Bib Gourmand.

The soup still comes to the table unseasoned. Salt, pepper and scallion sit beside it, and the seasoning is left to you.
